# Integration Controls Unveils New Buying Tool for Clients Addressing Industry Pain Points

Shop the Look aims to make the buying process more approachable for prospective integration clients by providing a ‘common vocabulary’ for project scope and pricing.

Published: September 21, 2026Nick Boever

![Photo of environment in Shop the Look](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ShoptheLook.jpg)

Photo courtesy of Integration Controls

Integration Controls is launching a new tool for its customers aimed at making the buying process for home technology upgrades much simpler. Calling it “Shop the Look,” Integration Controls says it’s a first-of-its-kind digital planning experience to help its clients understand what’s possible (and what it costs) before the design process begins.

“Consumers today expect to research major purchases before they ever schedule a consultation,” said Jamie Briesemeister, co-founder and CEO of Integration Controls. “At the same time, it’s often a challenge for those unfamiliar with technology to visualize how it will look and function in their home, with their aesthetic and lifestyle in mind.

“We asked luxury designers and builders in the St. Louis area which interior styles were most common, and we designed a resource that matches different styles, whether it’s Mid-century or French modern.  Shop the Look provides a consistent way to visualize personalized home technology solutions, bringing our clients’ concepts to life.”

## What Shop the Look Aims to Provide for Custom Integration

According to Integration Controls, Shop the Look allows homeowners to explore curated levels of home technology from the comfort of their home, office or while meeting with design/build professionals for a project.

The platform organizes home technology into categories and tiers that are more intuitive to the average buyer, from foundational one-room technologies to fully bespoke, whole-home systems. This further allows users to compare different levels of performance across different price points while also exploring how different systems will appear in a variety of home styles.

#### Why Integrators Should Take Note

While developed to improve Integration Controls’ own client experience, Shop the Look addresses a challenge familiar to integrators across the industry: translating complex technology systems into an experience clients can easily understand.

In a way, the tool works to establish a common vocabulary, sometimes even before the first consultation, by giving everyone a clearer understanding of available solutions, investment options and lifestyle outcomes, reducing uncertainty and establishing more realistic expectations in the process.

“We built Shop the Look to solve a challenge within our own business,” Briesemeister added. “The preliminary response we’ve received from our manufacturer partners and other integrators suggests this isn’t just our challenge—it’s an industry challenge. For over 20 years, we have led with ‘experience-first’ and now, we have the ability to help our clients visualize what that means earlier in the process.  It’s an opportunity to rethink how clients are introduced to technology, ultimately making the buying experience better for everyone.”

### Where to See Shop the Look

For anyone looking to explore the tool themselves, Shop the Look is available now at integrationcontrols.com.

However, the launch also coincides with the Grand Opening of Integration Controls’ new Technology Design Center, located at 10164 Watson Rd in Sunset Hills, Missouri. There attendees will get in-person access to Shop the Look.

On Friday, October 2, 2026, from 4 to 7 pm, a private VIP preview will host design/build partners, realtors, and other business connections to explore the design center and ‘Shop the Look’ in person.

This will be followed by a community-wide Open House on Saturday, October 3, 2026, for the Sunset Hills and surrounding communities to visit.

To RSVP or learn more about the event, readers are instructed to either [click here](https://integrationcontrols.zohobackstage.com/DesignCenterPublicGrandOpening#/) or reach out to Vickie Hayden at vhayden@integrationcontrols.com.

# Audio Advice to Grow Sales Team in Response to Further National Expansion

Following a period of significant company growth, Audio Advice will be adding and relocating several personnel to keep pace with service and expertise.

Published: September 21, 2026Nick Boever

![Sony RGB](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Sony-wallAudioAdviceShowroom-1.jpg)

Interior, Audio Advice Showroom. Photo courtesy of Audio Advice

Following a period of [significant company growth and market expansion](https://www.cepro.com/news/audio-advice-expands-national-footprint-with-acquisition-of-the-sound-room/621168/), Audio Advice has announced it will be “beefing up” its sales force to continue to provide the level of customer service and product expertise that has earned the firm its national reputation in both custom integration (CI) and consumer electronics.

As part of this growth, Audio Advice is adding two key salespeople to its [Miami location](https://www.cepro.com/news/audio-advice-adds-sound-components-to-growing-family-of-national-locations/627354/): Sebastian Simon and Aleksei Panov.

Simon is a Miami local with deep ties to the community, while Panov has served Audio Advice’s Charlotte location for many years. As part of this new position, Panov will relocate to support the growing Miami team under Simon. Audio Advice says his extensive background in premium A/V solutions will be an immediate asset to the rapidly expanding Miami customer base.

Concurrent with strengthening the Miami team, Audio Advice is also welcoming industry veteran Chad Fagin to its Charlotte location. Fagin brings several decades of specialized experience in both high-performance audio and advanced home automation. Audio Advice says his vast knowledge will further elevate the premium, custom-tailored experiences that Charlotte-area clients have come to expect.

#### Why Integrators Should Take Note

These strategic personnel moves represent Audio Advice’s ongoing approach to growth across North America, ensuring that, as the company expands, its customer service retains the same level of quality and care that a more local business would have.

“As home technology becomes increasingly sophisticated, Audio Advice recognizes that the foundation of an exceptional customer experience lies in the expertise of its staff,” says the company in a press release.

“By continually recruiting, relocating, and investing in top-tier talent like Simon, Panov, and Fagin, the company ensures that every customer—whether they are building a dedicated home theater, upgrading their two-channel audio system, or integrating full-scale home automation—receives unparalleled guidance and support.”

# Z-Wave Fall Summit Unveils Programming for 2026 Outing

The event will begin with the members-only Unplug Fest before opening to the public with a Z-Wave Demo and tour of ADT’s open standard concept house.

Published: September 21, 2026Nick Boever

![Shelly Wave Z-Wave Long Range](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/zwave_transparent-1000x550-1.png)

The Z-Wave Fall Summit is coming up for 2026, and ahead of the event, the Z-Wave Alliance (referred to as the Alliance) has released greater details on the programming for attendees, both confirmed and prospective. The event kicks off September 29 with the member-only Unplug Fest, where Z-Wave Alliance members can conduct informal device-to-device interoperability testing for Z-Wave and Z-Wave Long Range (ZWLR) products, collaborate with other developers and manufacturers, and exchange knowledge across the ecosystem.

Following Unplug Fest, programming opens to integrators, installers, developers and other industry professionals. The Fall Summit will run from September 29–October 1 in Boca Raton, Florida.

#### Why Integrators Should Take Note

The Z-Wave Fall Summit is a three-day conference that brings together commercial and consumer IoT industry experts, manufacturers and practitioners for sessions spanning industry trends, market opportunities and Z-Wave technical development.

## Information and Programming for Z-Wave Fall Summit 2026

### September 29

Upon opening to the public, programming for the 2026 Z-Wave Fall Summit opens with a Z-Wave Feature Demo led by Z-Wave expert Eric Ryherd (Dr. Z-Wave). The Alliance explains that the demo will cover several Z-Wave features in action, including SmartStart commissioning, ZWLR, simultaneous Z-Wave Mesh and Z-Wave Long Range operation on the same controller, and sub-Gigahertz operation.

The day will conclude with a welcome reception—presented by Fall Summit diamond sponsor ADT—and will include a panel session discussing how open standards are shaping the future of the connected home as well as an opportunity to tour ADT’s Callahan Family Home.

### September 30

On September 30, programming will open to include:

- What Consumers Really Want, hosted by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, senior smart home reviewer at The Verge, who will share what drives smart home purchase decisions, where consumers still encounter friction and which features matter most in everyday use.
- The Professional Installation Market, where new CEDIA research sets the stage for a conversation with professional integrators about changing customer expectations, common project challenges and new opportunities.
- Beyond the Single-Family Home, hosted by Jennifer Kent, SVP and Principal Analyst at Parks Associates, alongside leaders across multifamily, hospitality and PropTech to examine what it takes to deploy connected technology at scale and where commercial markets are creating new opportunities for Z-Wave.
- Preparing for the Next Wave of Cybersecurity Requirements, where experts examine the latest developments around Europe’s Cyber Resilience Act and the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark, what manufacturers need to do to prepare, and how Z-Wave’s architecture can help support compliance with both programs.

The day will conclude with an informal networking event that offers attendees the chance to continue discussions from the day, exchange ideas, and connect with colleagues from across the smart home and commercial IoT markets.

### October 1

The final day of Fall Summit will be dedicated to member-only Technical and Marketing Committee and Working Group sessions, giving Alliance members dedicated time to collaborate on ongoing initiatives and help shape priorities for the Z-Wave ecosystem.

#### Registration Details

Z-Wave Alliance members can register for the full Fall Summit for $699. Installers, integrators and non-members can register for $99. Non-Member registration includes access to the Z-Wave Feature Demo and opening reception on September 29 and the September 30 programming and networking event. Unplug Fest and the October 1 working sessions are exclusive to Z-Wave Alliance members.

The full agenda, registration and travel information are available on the [Z-Wave Fall Summit 2026 event page](https://z-wavealliance.org/eve/z-wave-fall-summit-2026/).

# TCL Expands Follow-Up to NXTFRAME Art TVs with More on Way

The A300L and A400U bring TCL’s art tv tech into a slim, flush-mountable design, with the A400U also incorporating TCL’s QD-Mini LEDs for greater picture quality.

Published: September 21, 2026Nick Boever

![TCL A300L Designer Series](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/A300L_Lifestyle_2rs.jpg)

TCL A300L Designer Series. Images courtesy of TCL

Coming out [IFA](https://www.ifa-berlin.com/), TCL has expanded its flush-mounted Designer Series in the U.S. with two new lines, the A300L QLED and A400U QD-Mini LED Series. Both series will run on Google TV and include TCL’s Art Library, which offers users the option to display artwork at no subscription cost on the TV when not in use, allowing it to blend into the background. The TVs also include multiple matte options and a flush mount included in the box to help them better blend in with a home’s design.

## A300L Specs and Features

![TCL A300L Designer Series](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/A300L_Lifestyle_People-scaled.jpg)

The A300L series comes in 55-, 65- and 75-inch models with an 85-inch model expected to arrive at an intermediate date. The 55- and 65-inch models measure 1.1 inches deep, allowing them to sit nearly flush against the wall. The 75- and 85-inch models still sport a slim profile, measuring 1.17 and 1.26 inches deep, respectively.

All models in the series come with an ultra-matte, anti-glare screen that is designed to reduce reflections while adhering to that canvas-like aesthetic. The series also come with off-white and light-wood magnetic frames that further help complete the look. Additional handcrafted options are also available through Laredo Factory Frames.

The screens themselves sport a 144 Hz refresh rate, according to TCL, with 4K UHD resolution that supports Dolby Vision, HDR10+, HDR10 and HLG formats. It also comes with a built-in 20W stereo system with Dolby Atmos and Dolby Digital+ processing. There’s also 3.5mm connector options for external audio.

## A400U Specs and Features

![A400U TCL Designer Series](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/A400U_Lifestyle_1-scaled.jpg)

The A400L series comes in 55-, 65-, 75-, 85- and 95-inch models with all models except the 95-inch sporting a screen depth of 1.6 inches. The 95-inch model comes in at 1.8 inches.

The A400U series keeps all the same art TV features of the A300L line with the main distinction being the QD-Mini LEDs, using TCL’s Halo Control System and Local Dimming Pro+ for improved backlight precision, contrast and blooming control.

The A400U also adds DTS:X spatial audio support.

#### Why Integrators Should Take Notice

The Designer Series is TCL’s follow-up to the NXTFRAME and NXTVISION TVs that originally marked TCL’s entry into the art TV category, now populated by the likes of Samsung, LG, SKYWORTH, Hisense, along with TCL.

While Samsung’s The Frame still stands as one of the gold-standards for lifestyle TVs in the custom integration (CI) channel, companies like SKYWORTH note the strong popularity of their own art TV offerings, highlighting the sheer popularity of the product category among integrators.

# WAC’s Spa-Ready TUCK Lights Arrive as More Connected Bath Solutions Enter the Channel

Already existing as outdoor luminaries, the TUCK, TUCK II and TUCK III have been updated with a heat-resistant model developed exclusively for saunas.

Published: September 17, 2026Nick Boever

![WAC Group Modern Forms TUCK sauna lights](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WAC-GROUP-FMW256605-TUCK-SAUNA_V21-scaled.jpg)

Image courtesy of WAC Group

#### Key Takeaways

- The TUCK, TUCK II and TUCK III feature a heat-resistant model for saunas.
- All three models provide upwards of 600 lumens at 3000K CCT and 90 CRI.
- The update arrives as new connected bath and spa solutions enter channel.

* * *

WAC Group is releasing a new set of spa-grade lighting fixtures via its Modern Forms lineup. The TUCK series, which already exists as an outdoor luminary, has been updated for spas and saunas with added heat resistance to an already wet-rated design. According to WAC Group, “Spa and sauna lighting has been needed for quite some time,” with the updated TUCK fixtures looking to address that need.

The lights themselves come in three different iterations, yet all share a similar circular profile defined by a diffuser with banded ring design, which, when lit, emits a soft, even glow designed to provide ambient illumination starting at 600 max lumens.

While the outdoor version of the TUCK lights offers four different CCT colorways, the sauna option is only available in 3000K. It is, however, heat resistant up to 185 degrees Fahrenheit and sports a 90 CRI. Additionally, the lights can be mounted either on ceilings or wall in all orientations.

The Sauna-ready versions of TUCK, TUCK II, or TUCK III are also ADA-compliant, Title 24-compliant and ETL-listed.

#### Why integrators should take note

While the custom integration (CI) industry is no stranger to specialty spa and sauna installs in the home, the 2026 CEDIA Expo put a particularly strong spotlight on the category as companies like Kohler and Thermasol have started to explore the channel more with connected bath solutions.

On its own, this would merit nothing more a curious intrigue, but both brands received considerable interest from integrators at the show, highlighting the appetite this channel has for being able to provide a connected sauna or spa solution. For this reason, _CE Pro_ has [identified the connected bath and spa as being a potential breakout category for integrators](https://www.cepro.com/news/custom-integration-dreams-of-a-connected-bath-may-finally-be-here/628640/) in the coming years given both homeowner and integrator interest.

And like other design-driven, wellness-focused spaces, lighting will ultimately sit as one of the pillars of experience.

# Devialet Unveils Pulse Blue Model for Phantom Ultimate Speaker

The new exclusive model revisits the brand’s original color identity while building upon the Phantom Ultimate’s audio architecture.

Published: September 17, 2026Nick Boever

![Devialet Phantom Ultimate Pulse Blue](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Devialet-Phantom-Ultimate_PulseBlue_KV_Product_1x1_Nuders.png)

Images courtesy of Devialet

#### Key Takeaways

- The Phantom Ultimate 98db – Pulse Blue revisits Devialet’s previously explored blue branding.
- The new Pulse Blue includes an extensive range of streaming protocols via AirPlay, Google Cast, Roon Ready, Spotify Connect, Tidal Connect, Qobuz Connect, and UPnP.
- The new edition and its matching Tree stand are available for pre-order starting today across all Devialet stores, on Devialet.com, and through authorized retailers.

* * *

One year after introducing the latest generation of its iconic speaker (and a few weeks after announcing a version [built specifically for custom integration](https://www.cepro.com/news/devialet-returns-to-cedia-expo-in-2026-with-phantom-ultimate-custom/628062/)) Devialet has an all-new, limited edition marked by a new finish: the Phantom Ultimate 98 dB – Pulse Blue. The new look and model are part of a partnership the company has with Global Brand Ambassador Isack Hadjar, a Formula 1 driver for Oracle Red Bull Racing.

Pulse Blue revisits the brand’s previously explored color identity, shifting the finish of the speaker’s side panels from matte to gloss with a mirror-polished surface. A clear varnish further enhances the deep RAL 5011 blue, creating a vibrant, light-responsive finish. The logo has also been refined for total visual coherence.

The new speaker also comes with a new stand to complete the look.

## The Tech Behind the Phantom Ultimate Pulse Blue

The Devialet Phantom Ultimate 98 dB – Pulse Blue builds on the Devialet DOS 3 software architecture while also integrating an extensive range of streaming protocols via AirPlay, Google Cast, Roon Ready, Spotify Connect, Tidal Connect, Qobuz Connect, and UPnP.

Beyond that, the Pulse Blue retains much of the original’s acoustic performance in a more compact form. The Pulse blue sports high-fidelity reproduction across frequency ranges from 18 Hz to 25 kHz (±6 dB), delivering up to 98 dB SPL.

An optimized audio chain supports files up to 24-bit / 192 kHz while a dedicated full-range driver broadens the acoustic field, to reproduce each note with precision and balance. Additionally, the Pulse Blue supports flexible listening in solo, stereo, or multi-room configurations, with compatibility across AirPlay, Google Cast, Roon Ready.

Through the Devialet app users can also access a 6-band equalizer to adjust frequencies as well as Bass Reducer and Loudness functionalities for added control over low-frequency intensity and improved acoustic compensation at lower volumes.

#### Price and Availability

The new edition and its matching Tree stand are available for pre-order starting today across all Devialet stores, on [Devialet.com](https://www.devialet.com/en-us/), and through authorized retailers, priced at $2,200 for the speaker and $349 for the Tree stand.

# Symphony of Old and New: Vintage Speakers Meet High-Resolution Audio in Brownsboro Smart Home

KLH electrostatic speakers serve as the centerpiece of this extensive audio project, with Mozaic Smart Technology Design adopting a hybrid system approach for a discerning client.

Published: September 17, 2026Nick Boever

![Featured Image](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/NeoclassicalVanguard-Mozaic.jpg)

Photos by Stephanie Johnson

When Mozaic Smart Technology Design took on this residence in Brownsboro, Alabama, the brief was simple: deliver top-tier audio in every corner of the home, from a dedicated theater to a fully distributed music system that matched with the client’s discerning tastes. However, part of that also involved finding a way to incorporate the homeowner’s vintage electrostatic speakers into the modern control ecosystem.

## Honoring electrostatic legacy without compromising performance

![A concealed subwoofer enclosure positioned beside the fireplace, discreetly reinforcing the low-end output of the vintage electrostatic speakers without disrupting the room's aesthetic.](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_6092-scaled.jpg)

The centerpieces of the project were the KLH electrostatic speakers, now decades old, that the client refused to part with. Beyond their size, the speakers carried deep sentimental value having been refurbished by David Janszen, son of the original designer behind the technology.

For Mozaic, the job was to make them the proud focal point of the main living area.

Elsewhere, Mozaic needed to get crafty to preserve the room’s sightlines while building out the system’s lower end to support the speakers. With no floor space to spare for subwoofers, the team designed concealed enclosures flanking the fireplace.

![](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/rack-2.jpeg)

In this way, the team paired cherished legacy components with new high-resolution equipment throughout the house, creating a hybrid audio architecture both aesthetically and technologically.

### From cinematic isolation to house-wide high-resolution audio

![lose-up detail of a JBL Synthesis speaker within the dedicated home theater, engineered for reference-level cinematic sound.](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_6050-scaled.jpg)

Moving into the home theater, Mozaic mechanically decoupled the room from the rest of the structure for true acoustic isolation. A 9.4.6 system built off JBL Synthesis speakers provides reference-level cinematic sound without a single decibel bleeding into the living spaces beyond.

Throughout the remainder of the house, Origin Acoustics speakers powered by AudioControl amplifiers drive the audio experience for the homeowners. Those whole-house speakers were chosen deliberately for their low-profile design, delivering acoustic performance while staying out of sight.

![Close-up view of a vintage KLH electrostatic speaker panel, showcasing its refurbished grille and slim architectural profile in the client's living room.](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_6040-scaled.jpg)

Tying it all together is an Autonomic streaming server, which feeds high-resolution tracks to every listening zone in the home.

“We embraced the complexity of a hybrid system. We expertly blended the client’s cherished components with new high-resolution audio equipment, ensuring aesthetic harmony and uncompromising sonic performance throughout the entire residence,” noted Michael Johnson, Founder and President of Mozaic Smart Technology Design.

![A cozy sitting room featuring discreetly integrated audio, blending high-performance sound with the space's warm, inviting design.](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_6077-scaled.jpg)

#### ![A wall-mounted touchscreen control interface installed beside a bookshelf, offering the homeowner intuitive access to the whole-home audio system.](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_2832-1.jpg)

#### Equipment list

##### Speakers

- JBL — SCL-2 — LCR loudspeaker (3, bi-amped)
- JBL — SCL-7 — Wide/side/rear surround loudspeaker (6)
- JBL — SCL-5 — Atmos in-ceiling loudspeaker (6)

- Origin Acoustics — D83 — Distributed audio speaker (8 pairs)

# LG Releases Statement Following Privacy Accusations Against Its Smart TVs

The initial report, released by the YouTube channel Gamers Nexus, claimed that LG smart TVs were being used to collect sensitive user data such as IP addresses and network devices.

Published: September 16, 2026Nick Boever

![LG Gaming Portal](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/AdobeStock_596228883_Editorial_Use_Only.jpeg)

Photo by roman - stock.adobe.com

#### Key Takeaways

- The YouTube Channel Gamers Nexus accused LG of using its smart TVs to gather sensitive user data through built-in microphones.
- LG’s response seeks to clarify “misconceptions” regarding the privacy and security of its TVs.
- LG argues that audio used for commands is processed locally by the TV.

* * *

LG is responding following a privacy accusation made against the company that it allegedly uses its smart TVs to spy on its users. The original accusation, made by the YouTube channel, Gamers Nexus, claimed that LG TVs can and are engaged in the collection of sensitive user information in a report that has since made the rounds online. In its statement, LG has declared that such reporting has led to “misconceptions about how smart TVs work,” while refuting many of the claims made in the original report.

## The initial Gamers Nexus report

In its initial report, [Gamers Nexus](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6IFVTcM28KA) alleged that LG smart TVs can record private conversations even when no wake word has been spoken. Additionally, the video accused the company of collecting sensitive data such as IP addresses, the geographic location of the TV and nearby Wi-Fi networks, as well as the names of all connected devices.

The report also included demonstrations of these claims in conjunction with Level1 Techs and independent cybersecurity researchers.

The report was followed by a massive uproar online with many consumers voicing their concerns over the potential invasiveness of smart TVs. Additionally, [prior statements made by LG](https://www.cepro.com/news/lg-subscription-ad-plans-tvs-thinq-appliances-energy/122880/) had begun to be picked over by those online, leading to greater furor and dissatisfaction.

### LG’s response to the privacy accusations

In its response, LG stated that “recent media coverage may have contributed to misconceptions about how LG smart TVs work,” with the company asserting that “LG smart TVs do not continuously record or transmit users’ conversations.”

“Speech-to-text processing begins only if a user activates a voice interaction through a supported wake-word feature or by pressing the voice (or AI) button on the remote control,” LG continues. “Audio used for wake-word detection is processed locally on the TV and, if no wake word is detected, audio is not converted to text, stored, or transmitted.

“Voice-recognition results and related technical logs may be generated as part of processing a voice command. These records are associated with specific voice interactions and do not indicate continuous recording of conversations occurring outside an active voice recognition session.”

The remainder of the response goes further into the functioning of the TVs in addition to clarifying data sharing policies and security measures.

The full privacy statement from LG can be found [here](https://www.lg.com/global/newsroom/news/statements/statement-understanding-privacy-on-lg-smart-tvs/?cjdata=MXxOfDB8WXww&cjevent=8aebb0f1b20411f1811c056d0a82b82c&utm_source=cj-affiliate-3486349&utm_medium=affiliate&cj_publishercid=3486349&utm_campaign=b2c_xbu_x_aon-cj-affiliat-text_cat_x_x_20211002&utm_content=dxp_en_%20x_15274760_x_x).

#### Why integrators should take note

Regardless of whether who is right in this circumstance, the discussion overall sours the public perception of smart TVs in many ways. And in much the same vein as one bad smart home experience can negatively impact the perception of the industry at large, so too can worries of privacy impact how much technology prospective integration clients will let into their homes.

As public accusations such as this make the rounds, it behooves integrators to be able to navigate conversations regarding data privacy with clients.

# Manufacturer Execs at CEDIA Expo 2026: The Future of Integration Is Relationships, Not Just Products

Channel leaders at CEDIA Expo 2026 outline the shift from products to experiences and installs to lasting client relationships.

Published: September 16, 2026CE Pro Editors

![Featured Image](https://www.cepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/CEDIA-Smart-Stage.jpg)

From left to right: Nick Berry, Michael Short, Melissa Andresko, Kathleen Thomas, Matt Kamp and Dan Ferrisi. Credits: CI Staff / Forge

Earlier this month at [CEDIA Expo 2026](http://cepro.com/tag/CEDIA-Expo-2026), five channel leaders told attendees that business is shifting from products to experiences, and from installs to relationships.

On the Smart Stage, a panel of manufacturer and distribution executives sat down to answer a deceptively simple prompt: what does custom integration look like five years from now and why.

The session, entitled “What Every Integrator Needs to Know About the Next Five Years,” brought together [Nick Berry, CEO of Origin Acoustics](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nick-berry-06a63b17); [Michael Short, global vice president of marketing operations and residential at Crestron](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/michaelshort1); [Matt Kamp, vice president of product management at ADI](https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthew-kamp-8937a025); [Melissa Andresko, chief corporate brand ambassador at Lutron](https://www.linkedin.com/in/melissaandresko); and [Kathleen Thomas, head of custom integration sales at Sony Electronics](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kathleen-thomas-ktstereo).

Dan Ferrisi, group director of content + editorial, industrial + tech, Forge, moderated the session.

The panel represented five different pieces of the custom integration channel: audio, control, distribution, lighting and displays. Nevertheless, three ideas united everyone on the Smart Stage: the selling experience has evolved, AI is a tool rather than a takeover and relationships with clients matter now more than the individual install.

Below, we take you back to the panel, offering a real-time recap of the live conversation and valuable insights shared by the panelists.

## Why Integrators Need to Pivot From Product to Experience

As the panel begins, Andresko frames the shift in the selling experience, remarking, “I think it’s going to be a lot less product-based and more experience-based.”

From her perspective, homeowners are no longer calling with a request for a specific product. They’re describing an outcome instead: a home that runs itself, a room that feels right, a life made simpler. She sums up where that leads in three words. “This concept of just invisible luxury,” says Andresko. That reframing changes what integrators sell and how they talk about it with clients.

Short sees artificial intelligence accelerating that same shift rather than working against it. He reveals that Crestron spent years building toward a single, standardized operating experience for every customer and AI is what lets integrators break from that uniformity again.

“I think now with AI coming, we’re going to be able to give a unique experience to everyone and put the power back into the integrator’s hands,” Short says. The tools get more capable, he observes, but the differentiation moves back to whoever is doing the install.

## AI as Tool, Not Takeover

Continuing the topic of AI, Short describes a practical use case already built into Crestron’s platform: automating the tedious front end of a project.

“So we’re showing ways within the platform that you can upload a floor plan from an architect of a 10,000 square foot home and the system then automatically builds all the rooms,” he says. According to Short, the pitch isn’t a smarter house; rather, it’s a faster setup, freeing integrators to spend that time elsewhere.

Berry also pushes back on the idea that AI leads to fully autonomous, sentient homes. “I think everybody’s mind is going to race to AI controlling the house and being living, breathing,” he says. “I don’t think that that’s necessary and I don’t think that that’s something that we should race to.”

Berry frames the technology instead as an efficiency layer, useful for diagnosing systems and speeding up service rather than a selling point on its own.

Thomas goes further, arguing AI can’t touch the part of the job that actually keeps integrators in business. “There’s no chatbot that’s gonna replace what I hear in conversations with integrators. That’s just not gonna happen,” she says.

## Lighting Has Its Time to Shine

In response to a question about which category has gone from niche to essential in the last five years, Andresko points to lighting. “Lighting was actually a number-one category,” she says.

Short goes a step further, framing lighting as close to a prerequisite for staying relevant with architects and designers. “Lighting is the gateway drug to many people’s hearts,” he says.

Andresko then extends the point beyond product into partnership, telling integrators to spend as much time cultivating architects and designers as they do clients. “Make yourself indispensable to builders, to designers \[and\] to architects,” she says.

## Security and Service: The Quiet Priorities for Integrators

Turning to other categories, Kamp names one that rarely gets top billing: cybersecurity. He explains, “I actually think cyber is going to be a really big part of what we all are responsible for over the next several years.”

Kamp describes security less as a product line and more as a baseline expectation that clients won’t think to ask about until something goes wrong.

Short raises a related priority: keeping systems running without a truck roll. “Systems are going to self-heal and AI again is going to help them actually figure out how to do service in a way that doesn’t mean picking up your phone and rolling a truck every other day,” he says.

Piggybacking off of Short’s remarks, Thomas notes that remote monitoring and other background services should also be available to integrators.

## Own the Relationship, Not the Project

The panel’s clearest through-line centers on the business model, not the technology.

Kamp puts it succinctly: “Own the relationship, not the project.” He then posits that integrators who treat every job as a one-time install are leaving recurring revenue, and loyalty, on the table.

Thomas’ advice is less about vision and more about discipline. “I have a deeply, deeply boring answer — learn to understand profitability,” she says, pointing to labor costs and service overhead as the numbers that quietly erode a margin that looks fine on paper.

Andresko frames the same shift in terms of the role, not revenue. She explains, “You are not just the provider. You need to change your mindset that you are an advisor.”

Thomas then takes that even further, flipping the tables on who’s actually the product. “\[A\]t the end of the day,” she says, “the _integrator_ is the product that they’re selling to the customer.”

## Turning Assumptions Around for Integrators

In the last segment, the panel turns to assumptions that the industry gets wrong, a path that brings the conversation in interesting directions.

For Thomas, a major assumption is that clients only care about price and features, not about quality. “Better stuff typically costs more. You typically make more money on it, but also the customer is getting a better value,” she says.

The idea that homeowners won’t pay for craft, in Thomas’ view, says more about how integrators pitch a job than about what clients actually want.

Berry focuses on a technical take that doubles as a sales pitch for talking to clients directly rather than defaulting to convention. Here, he points to how most installers default to the ceiling because it’s easier to sell and easier to hide and not because it actually sounds better.

“Speakers in the walls always sound better than in ceiling \[yet\] 95% of speakers go in the ceiling,” emphasizes Berry.

Andresko reiterates her stance on integrators needing to rethink and adapt their mindset. She adds that the integrator’s value today lies in “creating \[the\] magical moments for \[clients\] and their families, no matter where they are.” Berry agrees, proclaiming that the best recurring revenue is getting clients’ second and third homes.

Kamp then chimes in, declaring it as the “customer lifetime value.” He explains that measuring success is not “on the type of product or how much product we install, but the type of experiences we can deliver and the type of value that we can offer to the customer.”

## Integrators Repositioning Themselves

Summing up the conclusions, the panel’s five-year forecast isn’t about a specific device or platform. Instead, it’s about integrators repositioning themselves: from installers to advisors, from selling products to selling experiences, and from one-time jobs to relationships that last as long as the house does.

title: Europe’s electrification ambitions threatened by vote on steel
summary: Europe's electrification goals face significant challenges due to a proposed safeguard measure on essential grain-oriented electrical steel. Industry representatives warn that this measure could divert over €700 million annually from the transformer sector to only a few steel producers without guarantees for increased output. The absence of binding commitments for capacity expansion risks undermining both the competitiveness of the transformer industry and Europe's clean energy objectives.
content:
September 16, 2026

Share:

[Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Forgalim.eu%2Fen%2Feuropes-electrification-ambitions-threatened-by-vote-on-steel%2F&title=Europe%26%238217%3Bs+electrification+ambitions+threatened+by+vote+on+steel)

![](https://orgalim.eu/wp-content/uploads/Pylons.jpg)

# Europe’s electrification ambitions threatened by vote on steel

**This article has been updated since its original publication on Wednesday 16 September 2026. Please see below for the outcome of the vote.**

A major trade association that represents Europe’s grid technology industry, T&D Europe, and Orgalim are urging against the adoption of a safeguard measure for a type of steel needed in electrification.

Grain-Oriented Electrical Steel (nicknamed GOES) is a strategic material for transformers. Transfomers are an essential part of our energy infrastructure - and particularly our ambitions to electrify. The EU boasts strong domestic production of transformers, with manufacturing sites across 20 Member States, employing 23,000 people in quality, future-looking jobs.

Yet the future of this industry is under threat from a vote put to Member State representatives by the European Commission, scheduled to take place on Thursday 17 September.

> If adopted, the measure will transfer over EUR 700 million per year from the EU transformer industry, to just two domestic producers of grain-oriented electrical steel. And yet, there are no binding investment plans nor capacity commitments in place. It is deeply concerning.

\- Diederik Peereboom, T&D Europe Secretary General

Despite over a decade of the current GOES Minimum Import Prices scheme, EU producers still do not produce the highest-performing GOES, nor have they generated meaningful additional production capacity. Furthermore, the new proposal asks for no guarantees that EU GOES producers will expand output, add production lines, or develop the high-permeability and specialty grades that EU mills do not currently manufacture. In short, the measure will likely not add a single tonne of new EU GOES capacity online within its lifetime.

In contrast, the European transmission and distribution industry has invested heavily in domestic production. In the past 24 months, T&D Europe's 12 corporate members alone announced investments of EUR 12 billion in expanding global manufacturing capacity. The proposed measures would jeopardise the business case for these investments in Europe and imported transformers would become notably more competitive.

> The measure is presented as a balanced proposal that would not have significant implications for downstream industries. Yet, in reality, once again, it imposes a significant financial cost burden on a competitive and flourishing downstream industry – transformer manufacturing – that is essential to deliver Europe’s electrification ambitions, while rewarding upstream EU GOES producers without reasonable assurances that they will expand quantity and quality of GOES production in the years to come.

\- Ulrich Adam, Orgalim Director General

In place of this this safeguard measure, we propose policy measures in line with a value-chain approach, including:

- clear investment commitments by GOES producers to expand capacity and deliver high-performance grades; and
- regular structured dialogue with transformer manufacturers, TSOs and DSOs, and targeted industrial policy measures that strengthen the whole electrification value chain.

Both T&D Europe and Orgalim fervently support further development of a strong and competitive EU GOES industry. But support for GOES producers must not come at the expense of the transformer industry nor threaten Europe’s electrification ambitions.

When Europe’s electrification ambitions need speed, stability and long-term predictability, this proposal will instead:

- Reduce the ability of Europe's transformer industry to deliver on the needs of the growing demand for electrification, and to compete with non-EU imports both in the internal market and in markets outside the EU;
- weaken the attractiveness of the EU as an investment destination for critical, strategic, net-zero clean energy technology; and
- do little to expand quantity and quality of GOES production in years to come.

For these reasons, we urge against the adoption of these measures.

**About T&D Europe**

T&D Europe is the voice of Europe’s grid technology industry, representing more than 600 companies with more than 450 factories across the continent that design, manufacture, and supply the technologies underpinning Europe’s electricity networks. Employing over 175,000 people, the sector is a key enabler of the energy transition, supporting grid modernisation, renewable energy integration, energy security, and the EU’s objective of achieving climate neutrality by 2050.

**Update:**

Thursday 17 September, the Safeguards Committee delivered no opinion, meaning the measures were neither voted down nor approved by Member States. The outcome of the vote was 10 Member States in favour, while six voted against and 11 abstained. The European Commission can now either move ahead with temporary safeguards on transformer steel, or review the measure and resubmit it for a second vote.

Orgalim remains committeed to working with all partners across the European institutions and seeking an outcome that is beneficial for Europe's technology industries and demonstrates a holistic approach across the full industrial value chain.

title: Revising product rules to boost one of EU’s greatest strengths: the EU Single Market
summary: The article discusses the importance of revising product rules to enhance the EU Single Market, enabling easier cross-border trade and reducing costs for manufacturers. It highlights that a strong Single Market can boost competitiveness and innovation while ensuring consumer safety. The upcoming European Product Act aims to modernize regulations and strengthen enforcement for better compliance and accessibility.
content:
September 15, 2026

Share:

[Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Forgalim.eu%2Fen%2Frevising-product-rules-to-boost-one-of-eus-greatest-strengths-eu-single-market%2F&title=Revising+product+rules+to+boost+one+of+EU%26%238217%3Bs+greatest+strengths%3A+the+EU+Single+Market)

![](https://orgalim.eu/wp-content/uploads/EPA-Event-Article.jpg)

# Revising product rules to boost one of EU’s greatest strengths: the EU Single Market

**Wednesday, 9 September:** How quickly new products reach the market, and how easily European companies can sell across borders, and even the products available to us in the first place are all governed by a set of rules that are central to the running of the European Union's Single Market.

At its simplest, strengthening the Single Market makes it easier for a company to make a product in one European country, then sell it throughout the EU.

Having these common rules in place should remove barriers between national markets, reduce unnecessary costs and give manufacturers access to a market of hundreds of millions of consumers.

For European industry, scale matters. The Single Market is a phenomenal asset for the EU. If used well, it can help our companies grow, invest, innovate and compete globally.

The EU is currently looking at how to modernise and simplify the rules that underpin the Single Market, from standardisation and conformity assessment to market surveillance and product compliance. Much of this work will feed into the forthcoming European Product Act, alongside broader efforts to simplify EU rules and reduce barriers for businesses operating across Europe.

> We want to keep what works, while addressing gaps, making better use of digitalisation and strengthening enforcement.

\- Federica Boledi, Orgalim Policy Senior Manager - Internal Market

It was on these elements that Orgalim offered flash briefings to almost twenty APAs and attachés last week, looking at some of the technical rules for the Single Market and what they mean in practice.

Hosted by MEP Nikola Minchev, the event broke attendees into four groups, who moved from booth to booth to hear concrete examples in four key areas:

- How companies demonstrate that products meet EU requirements;
- how harmonised standards help ensure products can be placed on markets across Europe;
- how compliance information could become more accessible through digital documentation; and
- how market surveillance helps keep unsafe products off the market while ensuring fair competition.

> "These may sound like technical details, but they have very real consequences. For a manufacturer, clear and proportionate rules can mean less duplication, lower compliance costs and fewer obstacles when bringing a product to customers in another EU country.

\- Rocio Mondaca Gherardelli, Orgalim Policy Senior Adviser - Internal Market

For consumers meanwhile, effective rules help provide confidence that products are safe and meet the necessary requirements.

Feedback from participants at the Orgalim event stressed that the modular design of the briefings was enormously helpful for understanding the technical details of this complex package.

The European Product Act therefore offers an opportunity to look at whether the EU’s product framework is working as effectively as it could.

Getting this balance right matters. A strong Single Market is about removing barriers and creating the conditions for European businesses to compete, innovate and invest at scale.

The rules behind Europe’s products may be invisible to most people. However, getting them right can make a very visible difference to Europe’s economy and to the products people use every day.

title: Strengthening Europe’s Industrial Heartbeat: From Stockholm to Mannheim
summary: Orgalim leaders visited ABB's Mannheim campus to explore technologies for improving energy efficiency, finding that 60% of motors lack variable speed drives. A subsequent visit to Stockholm highlighted the need for cooperation among industry, research, and policymakers to enhance Europe's industrial competitiveness. The focus is on utilizing existing technology to close the deployment gap in advanced manufacturing and electrification.
content:
September 8, 2026

Share:

[Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Forgalim.eu%2Fen%2Fstrengthening-europes-industrial-heartbeat-from-stockholm-to-mannheim%2F&title=Strengthening+Europe%E2%80%99s+Industrial+Heartbeat%3A+From+Stockholm+to+Mannheim)

![](https://orgalim.eu/wp-content/uploads/Visits-Article.png)

# Strengthening Europe’s Industrial Heartbeat: From Stockholm to Mannheim

The human heart doesn’t beat at the same speed all the time. That would be inefficient. Rather, it speeds up when you run and slows down when you rest. This is the same principle that Orgalim member ABB applies to variable speed drives: a technology that can help optimise processes and improve energy efficiency.

Orgalim Director General Ulrich Adam, Senior Managers Stéphanie Mittelham and Federica Boledi, and Policy Manager Laure Dulière visited the ABB Campus in Mannheim recently to see first-hand the tangible technologies powering the green transition and learnt an important statistic: 45% of the world's electricity is converted into motion by electrical motors. Yet 60% of electrical motors still lack variable speed drives, massively reducing efficiency.

The visit was followed a few days later by a trip to Stockholm by Orgalim President Javier Ormazabal, Director General Ulrich Adam and Policy Director Daniel Wennick to meet with one of our prominent national members, Teknikföretagen, as well as Scania Group, and IVA. Discussions reinforced the importance of strong cooperation between industry, research and policymakers to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness and accelerate advanced manufacturing, electrification and innovation.

Both site visits emphasised the same point: the technology exists and is ready to use. The real challenge now is closing the deployment gap and improving Europe's industrial heartbeat.

![](https://orgalim.eu/wp-content/uploads/Town-Hall-Article-1.jpg)

# What We Do Matters: CEO Javier Ormazabal’s Town Hall Message to Orgalim

**Wednesday 2 September:** There was a familiar feeling in the air at Orgalim last Wednesday: the sense of a new beginning that comes with the start of a new school year and a return following the summer holidays.

For Orgalim President Javier Ormazabal, it was an opportunity to bring colleagues together, share some reflections from his own experience in industry and, above all, talk about the people behind Europe’s technology industries and the work they do every day.

Javier began with his own story. His family busines was founded in Bizkaia in 1967, during a period of rebuilding for the Basque Country. Visiting the company as a young man, he was struck by its constant sense of forward movement. This is a quality that remains central today.

What was advanced in his father’s time is no longer advanced today. The same factory is now home to entirely different technologies, systems and capabilities, and he discussed how this is a powerful reminder that progress depends on a willingness to keep learning, adapting and improving.

That spirit of curiosity connects Javier’s experience at Ormazabal with his role at Orgalim. Europe has an extraordinary industrial and technological base, he said, but this strength brings responsibility as well as pride. At a time when global competition is intensifying and Europe must decarbonise while remaining competitive, the challenge is to ensure that sustainability and industrial strength reinforce one another.

For Javier, this means being a strong and constructive voice for industry: speaking up when legislation risks undermining Europe’s ability to invest, innovate and manufacture, while also bringing practical solutions grounded in the realities of factories, laboratories and engineering departments.

The strongest theme of the Town Hall was people.

> Ambition is a contradiction. It is deeply personal, yet almost always makes you very dependent on others.

\- CEO Javier Ormazabal, Orgalim President

Javier stressed that a strong team is one where people are willing to engage, understand complexity, find solutions and show loyalty to their colleagues and their profession. The best organisations are those where people know they are not working alone, and understand that their individual contribution matters. After all, the policies and decisions taking place in Brussels ultimately affect factories, industries, regions, workers and families across Europe.

The Town Hall concluded with an engaging Q&A, giving colleagues the opportunity to put their questions directly to the President and continue the conversation.

title: Q&A: The EU ETS: Driving decarbonisation, while keeping Europe competitive
summary: The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) is the EU's primary tool for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, established in 2005. It operates on a cap-and-trade principle, covering about 40% of emissions and expanding to bring more sectors under its scope. The ETS promotes industrial decarbonisation while balancing climate ambitions with competitiveness through market incentives and technological investments.
content:
July 23, 2026

Share:

[Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Forgalim.eu%2Fen%2Fqa-the-eu-ets-driving-decarbonisation-while-keeping-europe-competitiveqa-understanding-the-electrification-action-plan%2F&title=Q%26amp%3BA%3A+The+EU+ETS%3A+Driving+decarbonisation%2C+while+keeping+Europe+competitive)

![](https://orgalim.eu/wp-content/uploads/Europe-map-1-e1784819881106.jpg)

# Q&A: The EU ETS: Driving decarbonisation, while keeping Europe competitive

##### What is the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and what role does it play in Europe’s climate policy?

The EU ETS is the **European Union’s carbon market** and its main tool for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Established in 2005, it works on a **‘’cap-and-trade’’** principle: the EU sets a limit on the total emissions allowed from covered sectors, and companies must surrender allowances for the emissions they produce. This creates a carbon price that encourages emissions reductions and investment in cleaner solutions.

The EU ETS is widely considered the centrepiece of EU climate policy and the world's **largest carbon market.** Today, it covers around **40%** of EU’s greenhouse gas emissions, including emissions from power generation, energy-intensive industries and aviation. Its scope is expected to expand significantly in the coming years as **additional sectors** are brought into the system.

##### What is the difference between ETS 1 and ETS 2?

The current system is referred to as **EU ETS 1,** covering sectors such as energy intensive industries, power generation and aviation. A separate system, **EU ETS 2,** will extend carbon pricing to buildings and road transport. Together, these systems are expected to cover around **70% of EU greenhouse gas emissions by 2028.**

##### How does the ETS support industrial decarbonisation, and why is it important for Europe’s technology industries?

The EU ETS supports industrial decarbonisation by putting a price on carbon emissions and creating incentives for companies to invest in cleaner production processes, energy efficiency and low-carbon technologies.

Orgalim considers the ETS a market-based, technology-neutral and cost-efficient tool that has played an important role in **driving investment in decarbonisation.** Europe’s technology industries are crucial to this transition, as they develop and supply many of the solutions needed to reduce emissions, including **carbon-neutral energy solutions, electrification technologies, advanced manufacturing systems and clean industrial equipment.**

> Orgalim considers the ETS a market-based, technology-neutral and cost-efficient tool that has played an important role in driving investment in decarbonisation.

\- Daniel Wennick, Policy Director, Orgalim

##### How can the ETS balance climate ambition with industrial competitiveness?

The EU ETS should continue supporting Europe’s climate objectives while ensuring a realistic pathway to decarbonisation. This requires a framework that supports innovation, enables industrial modernisation, provides the right investment conditions and addresses the risk of carbon leakage.

> EU ETS 1 should not reach zero emissions by 2039. Instead, the reduction pathway should be extended so that ETS 1 reaches carbon neutrality in the mid-2040s, while remaining aligned with the EU's 2050 climate neutrality target.

\- Daniel Wennick, Policy Director, Orgalim

In parallel, the phase-out of free allowances and the introduction of the **Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)** should be delayed to avoid putting excessive pressure on sectors exposed to international competition. This additional time should be used to strengthen CBAM, particularly its ability to prevent carbon leakage and protect European companies competing in global markets. **CBAM protection should apply not only to ETS sectors but also to downstream industries.**

##### What changes are needed in the ETS to ensure companies have the certainty, flexibility and investment conditions required to decarbonise?

Orgalim identifies several priorities:

- Create a predictable **long-term framework** towards 2040 and 2050 so companies can plan investments with confidence.
- Maintain a **technology-neutral approach**, enabling companies to choose the most effective solutions for emissions reductions.
- Increase the **use of ETS** revenues to support innovation and industrial modernisation through tools such as the Innovation Fund, Industrial Decarbonisation Bank and Modernisation Fund.
- Adjust the **Linear Reduction Factor (LRF)** to ensure a more realistic transition while reamining aligned with climate objectives.
- **Delay the phase-out of free allocation** for sectors exposed to global competition and **strengthen CBAM** to reduce carbon leakage risks.
- Include **permanent carbon removals** within the ETS framework.

The Commission's 2026 EU ETS review proposal includes several elements aligned with these priorities, including a lower post-2030 LRF, increased support for industrial decarbonisation through ETS revenues, the inclusion of permanent carbon removals and a delayed phase-out of free allocation for CBAM sectors.  However, extending the phase-out from 2034 to 2038 does not go far enough to provide the certainty and protection needed for industry.

##### How can Europe’s technology industries help deliver the goals of the ETS and support a competitive, climate-neutral Europe?

**Europe’s technology industries** are key enablers of the transition to a climate-neutral economy. They develop and manufacture the solutions needed to reduce emissions, including electrification technologies, clean energy systems, advanced manufacturing equipment and clean industrial technologies.

By investing in innovation, scaling up low-carbon technologies and supporting industrial modernisation, they can help reduce emissions while strengthening Europe's industrial competitiveness. Orgalim argues that a well-designed ETS should structurally support the **development** and **deployment** of these technologies by creating the right conditions for investment and helping Europe remain a **global leader** in clean manufacturing and climate solutions.

title: Q&A: Understanding the Electrification Action Plan
summary: The Electrification Action Plan is a European Commission strategy aimed at increasing electrification across various sectors to support decarbonization and enhance energy security. It addresses challenges such as electricity affordability and grid access while promoting existing technologies for efficient energy use. The plan seeks to bolster the competitiveness of European industries by providing a supportive and flexible framework for electrification investments.
content:
July 17, 2026

Share:

[Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Forgalim.eu%2Fen%2Fwhy-europes-technology-industries-are-key-to-the-electrification-action-plan%2F&title=Q%26amp%3BA%3A+Understanding+the+Electrification+Action+Plan)

![](https://orgalim.eu/wp-content/uploads/shutterstock_2550403129-scaled-e1784284209350.jpg)

# Q&A: Understanding the Electrification Action Plan

##### What is the Electrification Action Plan?

A political strategy designed by the European Commission to increase electrification of usages in Europe. The Plan includes a list of concrete measures (legislatives or not) aiming at stimulating the use of electricity for heating and cooling buildings, for transport and for manufacturing products and technologies.

Electrification has stagnated for a combination of reasons: The access to affordable, secure and stable electricity remains a challenge, and there is significant variation between Member States in terms of prices and infrastructure. At the same time, Europe is operating with ageing grids and still lacks a truly integrated Energy Union. Another challenge is that, after decades of subsidising fossil fuels,there is a need to better inform consumers about the technologies that already exist for electrification and those that are emerging in a continuous drive to find innovative solutions for more efficient and decarbonised energy use.

##### Why is the Electrification Action Plan particularly relevant now?

Electrification was initially driven by the need to decarbonise the economy, and it remains one of the fastest ways to achieve emissions reductions, particularly when combined with the deployment of renewable and low-carbon energy sources.

Today, it is a critical energy security issue. Europe's access to fossil fuels is increasingly unstable and our dependence on foreign governments comes at a significant cost. At the same time, investments in renewables and low-carbon energy have proven their value, meaning Europe is increasingly ready to rely on its own energy sources rather than imported fuels. This is why electrification is attracting so much attention today: it can support decarbonisation, improve energy security and help Europe become more independent.

##### What does the Electrification Action Plan mean for Europe's technology industries?

For many years, Europe's technology industries have invested in innovation, energy efficiency and technologies that support decarbonisation. As a result, we already produce many of the solutions needed for electrification. These technologies can help industries make better use of local renewable energy sources, participate in flexibility markets and adapt their energy consumption to price signals through smart and automated systems.

In addition, as well as supporting climate and energy objectives.

> Orgalim believes that the increased adoption and deployment of electrification technologies will strengthen the competitiveness of European industry by helping companies become more efficient, resilient and less dependent on external energy sources.

\- Laure Dulière, Manager - Energy, Climate and Innovation

##### If the technologies already exist, why isn't electrification happening faster?

For many industrial applications, especially low- and medium-temperature processes, electrification technologies are already commercially available. The two main barriers are:

1. Electricity prices

The business case for electrification often depends on access to affordable and predictable electricity prices. Many companies have faced significant price volatility in recent years, making investment decisions more difficult.

2. Grid access

Many industrial sites face challenges when connecting to the electricity grid or increasing their available grid capacity. In some cases, companies do not know when connection requests will be processed, creating uncertainty and delaying investment decisions.

While technology readiness is improving, these structural barriers continue to slow deployment.

##### How can the Electrification Action Plan help address these challenges?

The Electrification Action Plan can help in several ways. Firstly by sending a strong political signal that electrification is a key part of Europe's future industrial and energy strategy. This is important because it gives businesses greater confidence that investments in electrification are aligned with the long-term direction of EU policy.

Secondly, it can improve the business case for electrification by promoting measures that support electricity affordability and price stability. In particular, it can encourage greater flexibility in the electricity system and explore how network charges can better reward consumers that participate in flexibility markets or act as prosumers.

Finally, the Action Plan can help raise awareness of existing electrification technologies and support ongoing efforts to modernise the grid, ensuring that consumers and industries are better equipped to electrify their operations.

##### What would a successful Electrification Action Plan look like from Orgalim's perspective?

Although the Electrification Action Plan is a political strategy rather than a legislative proposal, we hope it will include concrete actions that accelerate electrification across Europe.

For Orgalim, success would mean greater electricity affordability and price stability, stronger support for industrial investments, and increased certainty for businesses considering electrification projects. This is particularly important when companies face high upfront capital expenditure costs.

We would also like to see a strong link between electrification and energy efficiency. Many electrification technologies can make industrial processes more efficient, so these two objectives should go hand in hand.

Ultimately, a successful Action Plan would create the conditions that allow industries to invest with confidence and deploy electrification technologies at scale.

##### What would Orgalim not like to see in the Electrification Action Plan?

Sector-specific or overly-prescriptive approaches thatr create strict obligations or additional burdens for companies would be a concern. While we support the electrification of our economy as extensively as possible, we must also consider that companies operate in different circumstances. Not all industrial processes can be electrified in the same way or at the same pace, so businesses need flexibility to identify the solutions that work best for them.

> The Action Plan should therefore provide an open and enabling framework rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

\- Laure Dulière, Manager - Energy, Climate and Innovation

At the same time, we believe that indicative EU-wide electrification targets could be useful to monitor progress and track Europe's electrification journey, provided they remain aligned with the EU's broader decarbonisation objectives and do not translate into rigid obligations for individual sectors or companies.

title: Europe’s industrial strategy GOES nowhere
summary: The EU's new steel tariffs aim to protect its producers, but raise concerns about their impact on downstream industries vital for electrification. This contradiction undermines the EU's industrial strategy, which should support innovation and long-term goals. Without addressing these issues, Europe risks damaging the very sectors needed for its clean technology future.
content:
July 7, 2026

Share:

[Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Forgalim.eu%2Fen%2Feuropes-industrial-strategy-goes-nowhere%2F&title=Europe%E2%80%99s+industrial+strategy+GOES+nowhere)

![](https://orgalim.eu/wp-content/uploads/GOES-news-article-picture.png)

# Europe’s industrial strategy GOES nowhere

On 1 July, new import quotas and tariffs on steel entered into force. The measures are intended to further protect European steel producers from persistent global overcapacity and unfair competition from non-EU producers. The theory being that steel is a strategically important industry, and that production must remain in Europe.

Yet the latest measures expose a much bigger question that the European Union must answer, as it tries to build a coherent industrial strategy. Namely, what counts as strategic?

Industrial policy requires choices. Europe cannot protect every single industry equally. But the choices must be guided by a coherent long-term strategy, rather than a series of ad hoc interventions.

Today, that coherence is increasingly difficult to see.

Resilience has come to mean one thing above all else: protecting selected upstream industries. This is often at the expense of downstream manufacturers who produce the technologies Europe says it wants to champion.

> We are facing an industrial policy that strengthens the weak but weakens the strong.

\- Ulrich Adam

The latest example is Grain-Oriented Electrical Steel (GOES).

Earlier this year, the European Commission launched a safeguard investigation into imports of GOES, opening the possibility of new trade restrictions, despite European production already falling well short of rising domestic demand.

At first glance, GOES appears to be just another technical trade case. In reality, it exposes a blatant and much broader inconsistency in Europe's industrial thinking.

GOES is the specialised electrical steel that allows transformers and large generators to operate efficiently by directing magnetic fields with minimal energy loss.

> Without GOES, there are no transformers. Without transformers, there is no expansion of Europe's electricity grid. And without grid expansion, there is no large-scale electrification of the economy – needed to free Europe from its costly and longstanding dependencies on imported fossil fuels.

\- Ulrich Adam

That makes the timing of the investigation particularly odd.

This week, European Commission is considering trade measures that will make one of electrification's most essential raw materials significantly more expensive and less accessible to European transformer manufacturers.

Next week, it is expected to publish its Electrification Action Plan: a roadmap intended to accelerate Europe's transition towards an electrified economy.

Taken together, both measures are in a complete contradiction, at a moment when Europe desperately needs strategic coherence.

The steel industry's concerns are real; we acknowledge that. European producers face high energy costs, intense international competition and the consequences of global overcapacity. Supporting European manufacturing capacity matters.

However, strategic thinking requires looking beyond the first link in the value chain. This seems to be something which the European Commission ardently refuses to do. Europe cannot afford to build a one-sided industrial strategy that shields selected upstream sectors from competition while expecting the rest of the value chain to absorb ever-rising costs, pay the bill, and continue producing.

No region can electrify with raw steel alone. It electrifies through transformers, generators, electric motors, and the countless technologies designed and manufactured by Europe's downstream industries. These are the companies that turn raw materials like steel into innovative cleantech products that make electrification possible.

At the same time, those manufacturers are being driven into the ground as supply of critical inputs like GOES becomes more expensive and uncertain. As a result, Europe's wider strategic ambitions will become harder to achieve.

This reflects a broader challenge in European industrial policy. The old industrial policy simply focused on protecting production capacity. The new industrial policy must focus on enabling innovation, strengthening cleantech production and supporting the industries that will define Europe's future competitiveness.

That requires a proper strategy that informs long-term thinking and sound tactical decisions.

It also requires recognising that not every sector is able to contribute equally to our long-term objectives. If Europe is serious about electrification, clean technology and strategic autonomy, then the industries enabling those goals must be recognised as strategic.

The manufacturers of transformers is one such industry. Europe's transformer manufacturers employ tens of thousands of people across dozens of production sites, supplying the equipment needed to modernise and expand Europe's electricity grid. Without their products, electrification simply can and will not happen.

The irony is difficult to ignore.

GOES has already benefited from trade protection since 2015, yet European production still cannot satisfy European demand. The product was excluded from previous safeguard measures precisely because of that structural shortage. If more than a decade of protection has not solved the underlying competitiveness challenge, it is reasonable to ask whether additional trade restrictions are really the answer, or whether they simply transfer costs onto the industries Europe most needs to succeed.

The Commission rightly argues that Europe cannot rely excessively on volatile international supply chains. But if resilience is defined solely through the lens of steel production, Europe risks weakening the very manufacturers that produce the technologies essential for electrification, decarbonisation, and energy independence.

Ultimately, industrial strategy is about making coherent choices. What does Europe really consider strategic?

If the answer is simply steel, then Europe risks protecting the input while undermining the industries that transform it into the technologies needed for the green transition to succeed.

If the answer is Europe's ability to electrify, reduce energy dependencies and compete globally, then strategic thinking must stretch beyond raw materials and duly consider the downstream manufacturers that make those ambitions possible.

> Europe undoubtedly needs a competitive steel industry. But it also needs affordable access to the specialised materials that power its clean technology industries to deliver Europe’s much broader strategic ambitions for electrification and greater energy security.

\- Ulrich Adam

**Otherwise, in trying to strengthen one part of the industrial chain, Europe risks weakening the very industries that will build its future.**
